title: TCP keeps the pieces in order
kid: Your phone and the video server number every little piece. If one falls in a hole, the phone keeps pointing at the gap until the server sends that piece again.
nerd: TCP is end-to-end (RFC 9293): a 3-way handshake (SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK) establishes sequence spaces. The sender keeps a four-segment window, ACKs advance it, and three duplicate ACKs for segment 5 trigger fast retransmit; delivery to the app waits for in-order bytes.

cdn.title: The server sends numbered TCP pieces
cdn.kid: The video server lines up pieces and lets four travel at a time. When your phone says piece 5 is missing, the server sends 5 again before the app gets the row.
cdn.nerd: From the server endpoint, TCP transmits segments with sequence numbers, observes cumulative ACKs, slides the send window, and fast-retransmits segment 5 after three duplicate ACKs without waiting for the RTO.

sealed.title: TCP passes by sealed
sealed.kid: This stop carries the numbered boxes, but it does not open them. It can see sealed piece 5 pass once, fall after the stop, and pass again when the server retries.
sealed.nerd: At this non-endpoint hop, TCP remains opaque: routers and bridges forward the IP packet and do not inspect sequence or ACK state. The retransmitted segment 5 is just another sealed payload passing through.

nat.title: A NAT only peeks at the port sticker
nat.kid: This box is still sealed here. The NAT only reads the tiny port sticker so replies can find the right phone, then leaves the numbered pieces alone.
nat.nerd: NAT is the exception to pure opacity: it reads and rewrites the TCP/UDP port tuple (for example 51034 ↔ the outside mapping) while leaving sequence numbers and data semantics end-to-end.

label.ready: all in order — ready for the app!
